opus-5.5.text:
It honestly feels a little bit like magic, and a little bit like talking to biology in its own language for the first time. You know, with language models for text, you prompt it with a sentence and it completes the thought. With Evo, you're prompting it with DNA sequence, the actual code of life, and it's completing that in a way that's biologically meaningful. You give it the beginning of a gene or a regulatory element, and it generates something that, when you go into the lab and test it, actually folds, actually functions.

The moment that really struck me was when we started seeing it generate entire systems, not just single proteins. Things like CRISPR-Cas complexes where the protein and the guide RNA have to work together, or toxin-antitoxin pairs, multi-component machinery that has to be co-designed. That's something that's really hard to do with protein-only models, because biology doesn't operate one molecule at a time. It operates at the level of genomes, of interacting parts across the central dogma: DNA, RNA, and protein all talking to each other.

So using it feels less like using a tool and more like collaborating with something that has read a huge fraction of the evolutionary record and absorbed some of its grammar. It's not perfect. It still hallucinates, a lot of what it generates doesn't work, and we're very early. But you get these glimpses where it's clearly learned something deep about how life is organized. And for a scientist, that's thrilling, because it suggests we might move from reading and editing genomes to actually writing them, designing biology at a scale that just hasn't been possible before.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it feels like gaining a new kind of intuition for biology. For most of my career, working with DNA meant reading and editing it piece by piece, with a slow design loop. You'd form a hypothesis, build something, test it, and wait.

With EVO, there's this shift where the model has absorbed so much evolutionary sequence that it starts to feel like it has a sense of what "looks like life" and what doesn't. You can give it a prompt and it generates sequences that are plausible, coherent, functional-seeming, almost like it's learned the grammar of genomes.

What strikes me most is the fluidity. You can move across scales, from individual molecules up toward whole genomic context, and the model holds some sense of how the parts fit together. It's less like running a single experiment and more like having a conversation with evolution itself. You ask, it proposes, you refine.

It's humbling too, because it surfaces patterns we never explicitly taught it. That's the exciting and slightly eerie part: it reflects structure in biology we're still working to understand ourselves.

astra-6.text: It feels a bit like having an autocomplete for DNA. You give it a stretch of sequence, and it predicts what might come next. But the exciting part is asking whether it has learned enough about biology to generate something that actually works. You can go from a sequence on a screen to an experiment in the lab and test that. That connection between generating a possibility and measuring its function is what makes it so compelling to me.
